Examiners reward specific place names and the link between process and landform. Avoid listing without explaining why each landform is there.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Glaciers deposit till (unsorted, directly from ice) and outwash (sorted by meltwater). Erratics (Norber, Yorkshire Dales) are rocks carried hundreds of kilometres from their source; drumlins (Eden Valley) are streamlined till mounds aligned with ice flow.
  • Four moraine types mark stages of glacial activity: lateral (valley sides), medial (where glaciers merge), terminal (furthest advance) and recessional (pauses in retreat).
  • The Lake District shows a complete glacial landscape: erosional landforms (Red Tarn corrie, Striding Edge arête, Windermere ribbon lake in a glacial trough, Aira Force hanging valley waterfall) alongside depositional landforms (Eden Valley drumlin swarm, moraines across the lowlands, Bowder Stone — a large andesite boulder traditionally cited as an erratic but now interpreted as a rockfall from Bowder Crag above).

lessons.title: Glaciated Uplands: Economic Activity, Conflict & Tourism
lessons.description: How the Lake District's glacial landscape is used, and how tourism, farming and conservation compete.
lessons.content_html:
Economic Activities in Glaciated Uplands

Glaciated uplands like the Lake District are not museum pieces — they support real economies. Four main economic activities operate in these landscapes, often in the same valleys, and often in direct competition with each other and with conservation.

Tourism is by far the dominant economic activity in most UK glaciated uplands. The Lake District receives around 18 million visitors per year, making it one of England's most visited destinations. Tourism generates approximately £2.4 billion for the local economy annually and supports around 16,000 jobs. Activities include walking and fell-running on the high fells, water sports on the ribbon lakes, cycling, rock climbing, holiday cottages, hotels and visitor attractions. The scenery — glacially carved corries, arêtes, U-shaped valleys and ribbon lakes — is the primary draw. The Lake District was designated England's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017, recognising the cultural and natural landscape.

Farming has shaped the Lake District for thousands of years. The thin, acidic glacial soils on the fell slopes are suited only to pastoral (livestock) farming — primarily Herdwick sheep, a breed so hardy it stays out on the fells year-round. The flat valley floors covered in ground moraine support more productive lowland farming — hay meadows, dairy cattle and market gardening in the Vale of Keswick. Farming maintains the open landscape that tourists come to see: without sheep grazing, the fell slopes would revert to scrub and woodland.

Forestry: the Forestry England estate manages extensive conifer plantations in parts of the Lake District, particularly around Grizedale Forest and Ennerdale. These produce commercial timber but have attracted controversy since mid-20th century plantings of non-native Sitka spruce in geometrical blocks were widely seen as visually intrusive and damaging to biodiversity. More recent management aims to restore native oak and birch woodland, and Ennerdale has undergone a major rewilding project removing conifers and allowing natural forest regeneration since 2003.

Quarrying has a long history in the Lake District: Honister Slate Mine, still active near Borrowdale, produces the distinctive blue-green Westmorland green slate used for roofing and paving across Britain. Quarrying provides skilled local employment but creates noise, visual intrusion and heavy lorry traffic on narrow valley roads. Tension between the quarrying industry and conservation authorities is an ongoing feature of Lake District management.

Key Fact

The Lake District receives around 18 million visitors per year, generating approximately £2.4 billion and supporting 16,000 jobs. The four main economic activities are tourism, farming (Herdwick sheep), forestry and quarrying (Honister Slate Mine).

Land Use Conflicts

With so many competing uses in a finite, protected landscape, conflict is inevitable. Land use conflicts in the Lake District fall into two main categories: conflicts between different users, and conflicts between development and conservation.

Between users: walkers vs mountain bikers on narrow fell paths — mountain bikes damage soft upland paths faster than boots; motorists vs cyclists vs hikers on the B5289 through Borrowdale, one of the Lake District's most scenic but narrowest valley roads; power-boat users vs canoeists and swimmers on Windermere — the 10 mph speed limit introduced on Windermere in 2005 resolved this conflict by banning fast powered craft, to the anger of water-ski operators but the relief of quieter users; tourists vs local residents — holiday cottage demand has pushed house prices far above local wages, with the average Lake District house price in excess of £300,000 and local workers unable to afford to live in the communities where they work.

Between development and conservation: new visitor facilities vs scenic landscape — any new car park, hotel or visitor centre must be approved by the Lake District National Park Authority, which weighs economic benefit against visual impact; sheep farming vs vegetation recovery — sheep overgrazing on the high fells has degraded upland habitats and reduced biodiversity; some ecologists argue fencing areas off and reducing sheep numbers would allow blanket bog and native scrub to recover, but farmers argue this destroys livelihoods and the open character of the landscape; quarrying vs national park principles — the Honister Slate Mine sits within the national park boundary, so any expansion requires special consent.

Before 2005, Windermere had no speed limit and was one of the few lakes in England where powered water-skiing and powerboat racing were legal. Quiet users — canoeists, rowers, wildlife watchers, swimmers — complained of noise, waves and safety risks. The Lake District National Park Authority introduced the 10 mph limit after a lengthy consultation. Water-ski operators and powerboat clubs lobbied hard against it, arguing their businesses and traditions were being destroyed. After the ban, the lake became noticeably quieter; nature tourism and wildlife-watching grew. This is a classic example of a management decision that pleased some users and angered others — and shows how the national park authority must balance competing demands.

Tourism in the Lake District: Attractions, Impacts and Management

The Lake District attracts tourists primarily for its physical landscape — the glacially carved scenery of fells, corries, arêtes, U-shaped valleys and ribbon lakes that cannot be found at this scale anywhere else in England. Secondary attractions include: the literary heritage (William Wordsworth's Dove Cottage at Grasmere; Beatrix Potter's Hill Top farm near Hawkshead); outdoor sports (Scafell Pike, England's highest mountain at 978 m, attracts tens of thousands of summit attempts each year); water sports on Windermere and Ullswater; and the network of narrow-gauge heritage railways.

Social impacts: local house prices inflated by second-home and holiday-let demand; seasonal overcrowding in honeypot villages like Grasmere, Bowness and Keswick in summer; language and cultural tensions as incomers from cities change the character of local communities. Economic impacts: tourism revenues keep small businesses, pubs, hotels and rural services viable; seasonal employment (low unemployment in summer, higher in winter); income for local farmers through farm diversification (bed and breakfast, glamping). Environmental impacts: severe footpath erosion on popular routes — Helvellyn's Striding Edge and Scafell Pike paths are deeply rutted by millions of boots; water pollution from boats and camping; increased litter and parking pressure in honeypot villages; disturbance of ground-nesting birds such as golden plover and dotterel on high fells.

Key Fact

Footpath erosion is the most visible environmental impact of tourism in the Lake District. The Fix the Fells project has restored over 400 km of upland paths since 2001, using helicopters to fly stone to remote locations and volunteer footpath workers.

Management Strategies

The Lake District National Park Authority and partner organisations use a range of strategies. Fix the Fells (established 2001) is the flagship upland path restoration project — volunteers and professional workers repair and harden eroded footpaths using local stone, pitching the path surface to drain water and withstand heavy use. Since 2001 over 400 km of paths have been restored at a cost of around £2,000–5,000 per 100 m. Traffic management: park-and-ride schemes operate at Bowness (Windermere) and Grasmere in summer; the Keswick to Threlkeld trail converts an old railway line into a traffic-free cycling and walking route. The 10 mph speed limit on Windermere (2005) manages water-use conflict. Sustainable tourism promotion: the national park authority encourages visitors to travel by bus and ferry rather than car — the Windermere Ferry and Borrowdale bus service are marketed as tourist attractions in themselves. Honeypot management: car park pricing, visitor information centres and interpretation boards spread the load and manage expectations. Conservation agreements with farmers (agri-environment schemes) pay Herdwick sheep farmers to reduce grazing on the highest fells, allowing heather and bog cotton to recover.

On the most remote fells — Helvellyn, Great Gable, Scafell Pike — there is no road access, so stone cannot be brought in by lorry. Fix the Fells uses helicopters to fly net-loads of locally sourced stone to the work site, at a cost of several hundred pounds per flight. Teams of path workers then pitch the stone by hand into the path surface, angled to drain rainwater off the sides rather than channelling it down the centre (which causes erosion). On less remote paths, volunteers carry stone by hand up the fell or use ponies. The aim is not to make paths look artificial — stone blends into the fell over a few years — but to stop the erosion cycle where a wet, churned path gets wider every year as walkers step around the mud.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 9-mark questions on tourism management in a glaciated upland, use the Lake District throughout and structure your answer around the three impact categories (social, economic, environmental) before moving to management responses. The strongest answers link a specific impact to a specific strategy: footpath erosion on Helvellyn → Fix the Fells (400 km restored since 2001); water-use conflict on Windermere → 10 mph speed limit (2005). Figures make answers stand out: around 18 million visitors, £2.4 billion economic value, 978 m Scafell Pike.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Lake District supports four main economic activities — tourism (around 18 million visitors, £2.4 billion/year), farming (Herdwick sheep), forestry (Grizedale, Ennerdale) and quarrying (Honister Slate Mine) — which frequently conflict with each other and with conservation.
  • Tourism brings social (house price inflation), economic (16,000 jobs) and environmental (footpath erosion, water pollution, disturbance of nesting birds) impacts; honeypot villages like Grasmere and Bowness bear the greatest pressure.
  • Management strategies include Fix the Fells (400 km of path restored since 2001), the Windermere 10 mph speed limit (2005), park-and-ride schemes, agri-environment payments to farmers and promotion of sustainable transport.

practice_questions.text: Describe the economic and social impacts of tourism on the Lake District.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: economic — around 18 million visitors per year; £2.4 billion contribution; 16,000 jobs; keeps rural businesses, pubs and hotels viable; farm diversification (B&B, glamping); seasonal employment pattern. Social — house prices inflated by second homes and holiday lets (over £300,000 average); seasonal overcrowding in honeypot villages (Grasmere, Bowness, Keswick); local workers priced out of communities. Named figures throughout. Secure: two impacts per category. Developing: lists impacts without figures. Emerging: only one category.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Lake District attracts so many tourists.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three types of attraction linked to cause — glacially carved landscape (corries, arêtes, U-shaped valleys, ribbon lakes) uniquely concentrated in a small area; England's highest mountain (Scafell Pike, 978 m) draws walkers and climbers; ribbon lakes (Windermere, Ullswater) for water sports and scenic cruises; literary heritage (Wordsworth, Beatrix Potter); UNESCO World Heritage Site status (2017) promotes international tourism; accessibility from major northern cities (Manchester, Leeds, Newcastle). Secure: two attractions with explanation. Developing: lists attractions. Emerging: 'it's beautiful'.

practice_questions.text: Suggest how land use conflicts can be managed in glaciated uplands.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three strategies with the mechanism of how they manage conflict — Fix the Fells (established 2001, path restoration with helicoptered stone, pitching surface to drain water, prevents erosion widening, 400 km restored); 10 mph speed limit on Windermere 2005 (separated powered and quiet water users, reduced noise and waves); park-and-ride at Bowness and Grasmere (reduces car numbers in honeypot villages); agri-environment payments (pay farmers to reduce upland grazing, allowing habitat recovery); planning controls (national park authority must approve new visitor facilities). Each strategy linked to the conflict it resolves. Secure: two strategies explained. Developing: lists strategies. Emerging: vague reference to 'rules'.

practice_questions.text: 'Tourism does more harm than good in glaciated upland areas.' Assess this view using a named example.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument using Lake District throughout, with a justified judgement. Against tourism (it does harm): footpath erosion on Striding Edge and Scafell Pike (heavily rutted, widening paths); water pollution from motorised craft and camping; house prices pushed above local wages (over £300,000), pricing out residents; seasonal traffic gridlock on narrow valley roads; disturbance of ground-nesting birds. For tourism (it does good): around 18 million visitors generate £2.4 billion and 16,000 jobs; keeps rural pubs, hotels and services viable; management strategies have worked (Fix the Fells restored 400 km of paths since 2001; 10 mph limit succeeded on Windermere); UNESCO status brings global prestige. Reaches a justified judgement — tourism is essential to the local economy but must be actively managed to avoid long-term environmental damage; the evidence from Fix the Fells shows that good management can reverse harm. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: general.
